title: On the Measure of Intelligence (ARC)
hook: Is a high benchmark score the same as intelligence? Chollet argues no — intelligence is how efficiently you acquire new skills, not how well you perform known ones.
key_points: Defines intelligence via algorithmic information theory: skill-acquisition efficiency, not raw performance.
Argues skill-based benchmarks reward priors and experience rather than generalization.
Introduces the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC), a few-shot reasoning benchmark.
ARC is built on human-like innate priors, testing learning rather than memorized skill.
content_html: François Chollet argues that the field has been measuring the wrong thing. A system that scores well on a task may simply have been trained on enough data to cover it, which says little about its ability to handle something new. He proposes a formal definition grounded in algorithmic information theory: intelligence as skill-acquisition efficiency, not raw task performance. To test that idea, he introduces the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC), a few-shot benchmark built on human-like innate priors.
extra_html:
How it works

Chollet frames intelligence in information-theoretic terms, treating it as how efficiently a system converts prior knowledge and a little experience into new skills. From that lens, ordinary skill-based benchmarks are misleading: they reward whatever priors and experience were baked in during training rather than the capacity to generalize. ARC is his counter-proposal — a set of abstract, few-shot reasoning puzzles grounded in priors humans seem to have innately, so doing well requires learning the rule from a handful of examples rather than recalling a memorized skill.

Why it matters

This reframing pushed the conversation past leaderboard-chasing toward generalization and sample efficiency as the real targets. ARC became a durable, deliberately hard challenge for that goal. A successor, ARC-AGI-2, arrived in 2025, and frontier models only began making real progress on it in 2025 and 2026 — a sign of how stubborn genuine few-shot reasoning has been, and why Chollet's distinction still resonates.

related.hook: What makes a question hard for a model? GPQA's are hard even for skilled people with Google: non-experts reach only 34% after 30+ minutes of searching.

related.title: MMLU: Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding
related.hook: Want one number for how broadly an LLM 'knows stuff'? MMLU is a 57-subject exam spanning history, law, medicine, and math — and it became a default yardstick.

flashcards.prompt: Why does Chollet argue ordinary skill-based benchmarks are misleading?

choices.text: They reward priors and experience baked in during training, not generalization
They are too small to be statistically valid
They only test memorized facts, never skills

flashcards.prompt: What does ARC require a solver to do?

choices.text: Learn the rule from a handful of examples, using human-like innate priors
Recall memorized skills from web-scale data

flashcards.explanation_html: ARC's few-shot puzzles are grounded in priors humans have innately, so success requires learning the rule, not recalling a skill.
